# Localizing Korean Content at Global Scale
## "Sell the Koreanness. Localize the access to it, not the artifact."

---

## 1. Diagnose: this is four budgets wearing one label

"Localization budget" collapses four economically distinct activities with wildly different cost curves and different jobs to do.

| Dial | What it buys | Cost per title-hour (index) | Job |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Comprehension** (subtitles, on-screen text, forced narratives, metadata) | Basic legibility of the work | 1× | Table stakes; failure here is silent and lethal |
| **Performance** (dubbing, ADR, mix) | Access for non-reading or dub-habituated audiences | **15–30×** | Audience *expansion* into new demos |
| **Cultural context** (glossaries, notes, advisory review, compliance versions) | Retention of meaning across a 5,000-year reference set | 0.3× | Prevents "I don't get it" churn; protects brand |
| **Fandom & discovery** (artwork, titling, creator programs, clip policy, launch orchestration) | Someone actually pressing play | Variable | Determines whether the other three get amortized |

**The arithmetic that governs everything:** a 16-episode K-drama subtitles into **30 languages for roughly the cost of dubbing it into 2**. Dubbing one 16-hour series into ten languages runs $2–3M; subtitling it into thirty runs $300–500k.

So the strategy is not "how much do we spend on localization." It is:

> **Subtitle everything, everywhere, at a quality level well above industry norm. Dub selectively, late, and on evidence.**

**The second insight — the asset thesis.** The reason Korean content travels is that it is *conspicuously Korean*: the honorifics, the food, the workplace hierarchy, the specific melodrama grammar. Every adaptation edit that sands this down destroys the thing being purchased. Hollywood spent thirty years learning this in reverse. Therefore:

> **Cultural distance is the product, not the defect. Never adapt the text. Add context around it.**

---

## 2. Invariants vs. the configurable layer

**Invariants — identical in every market:**

- **No narrative edits.** No re-scripting for cultural comfort. Only three permitted interventions (see §5's edit gate), all logged and disclosed.
- **Day-and-date global release.** Same hour worldwide (anchored to Korean drop time). Staggered releases are a piracy subsidy and a spoiler weapon against your own fandom.
- **One canonical Korean-source style bible** per franchise: honorific policy, name romanization, food terms, kinship terms, formality register mapping. Translation flows from Korean, never relayed through English pivot scripts.
- **Subtitles ship in every supported language at hour zero.** Non-negotiable. A market that gets subtitles two weeks late has already been fansubbed.
- **Korean audio is always available and never removed.** Track selection is a user choice, never a market default that can't be overridden.
- **Creator/partner approval** on the cultural advisory record for any compliance version.

**Configurable per market (the "Localization Profile"):**
Dub tier and language, subtitle register (literal / naturalized / fan-grade), default audio track on first play, glossary depth, artwork and title treatment, marketing archetype, fandom program intensity, compliance version existence, release-hour messaging.

**Rule:** a market receives a different *configuration of tracks and context*, never a different *cut of the show*.

---

## 3. The dubbing allocation engine — where the money actually goes

### 3.1 Dubbing is an option, not a commitment

Most platforms dub at greenlight or at launch — before they know if the title works. That is buying insurance on every car in the lot. Instead, treat every dub as a **call option exercised on observed demand**.

**Three-gate release cadence:**

| Gate | Timing | What ships |
|---|---|---|
| **T0** | Global drop hour | Korean audio + subtitles in all 30+ languages, localized artwork/metadata, context layer live |
| **T+7 to T+10** | After first-week signal | Dub greenlight decisions fire for Tier-1 languages already pre-booked in "warm" studio capacity |
| **T+21 to T+35** | Dubs land | Dub launch treated as a **second marketing moment**, with its own campaign to a distinct audience |

The T+30 dub drop is not a failure of speed — it is a **second bite at the launch**, reaching an audience segment (older, family co-viewing, second-screen, non-reading) that would not have converted at T0 anyway. Marketed properly, dub-drop weeks in Brazil, Thailand, Türkiye and Germany routinely out-perform the original launch week for that language.

**Exception — pre-committed day-one dubs:** reserve for ~4–6 titles/year with a hard prior (returning season of a proven hit, top-tier IP, franchise star). Everything else earns its dub.

### 3.2 The greenlight score

For each (title × language) pair:

```
Dub Score = (Reachable non-sub audience) × (Observed T+7 title velocity) 
            × (Dub-preference coefficient) × (Expected catalog tail)
            ÷ (Fully-loaded dub cost in that language)
```

Greenlight if projected **incremental viewing hours per $1,000 of dub cost** clears the market's threshold, and if projected incremental contribution (retention-saved + acquisition-attributed) exceeds dub cost within **18 months** — dubs are catalog assets with long tails, so an 18–24 month payback window is correct, not a quarterly one.

**Dub-preference coefficients** (rough, calibrated annually from track-selection telemetry):

| Cluster | Markets | Coefficient | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Dub-obligate** | Brazil, Mexico/LatAm, Germany, Italy, Spain, France, Türkiye, Thailand, Philippines (Tagalog), Indonesia, Japan | 0.85–0.95 | Dub is the default consumption mode; subs serve a minority |
| **Dub-elastic** | Vietnam, Egypt/Gulf (Arabic), Poland, India (Hindi/Tamil/Telugu) | 0.5–0.7 | Growing dub demand; format matters (Poland: lector) |
| **Sub-native** | Nordics, Netherlands, Portugal, Greece, Malaysia, Singapore, urban Korea-fandom cohorts everywhere | 0.1–0.2 | Dubbing here is largely wasted spend and reputationally negative |

Note the sub-native cohort exists *inside* dub-obligate markets: the 18–28 K-drama superfan in São Paulo watches in Korean with Portuguese subs and considers the dub an insult. This is why **default track selection must be personalized, not market-set** — infer from prior track behavior, not geography.

### 3.3 Three dub quality tiers — stop buying one grade of everything

| Tier | Spec | Cost index | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **T1 – Prestige** | Full lip-sync, name talent, Korean-fluent dub director, cultural consultant on script adaptation, 5.1 mix | 1.0× | Top 10 titles/year in top 6 dub-obligate languages |
| **T2 – Standard** | Lip-sync, professional cast, standard adaptation pass, stereo | 0.5–0.6× | The workhorse; ~70% of dub volume |
| **T3 – Access** | Voice-over/lector, or AI-assisted synthetic dub with **human casting, human direction, human QC and full performer consent/licensing** | 0.1–0.2× | Long-tail catalog, unscripted, variety, Tier-3 languages, back-catalog revival |

T3 is where the budget breakthrough lives — but it is **strictly fenced**: never on a T1 title, never on scripted drama in a market where the dubbing sector is unionized and politically visible (Brazil above all), always disclosed in the audio track name, always with consented voice licensing. Getting this wrong triggers a fandom-plus-industry backlash worth more than the savings. Treat AI dubbing as *catalog reactivation*, not as a substitute for premium dubbing.

### 3.4 Korean-specific dubbing craft problems

Budget must explicitly cover, or the dub fails:
- **Honorifics and formality shifts.** The plot point where a character switches from 존댓말 to 반말 is a dramatic beat. Languages with T-V distinction (Spanish, French, German, Portuguese, Turkish) can carry it; English and Thai need directorial solutions. This must be in the adaptation brief, not left to a dub writer.
- **Syllable density.** Korean is compact; Spanish and Arabic expand 15–25%. Under-budgeted adaptation produces rushed, unnatural dubs — the #1 driver of "dub sounds cheap."
- **On-screen text volume.** K-dramas are text-heavy (KakaoTalk overlays, news chyrons, signage). Forced-narrative subtitles or localized graphics are a real line item and are routinely under-scoped by 40%.
- **Kinship terms.** *Oppa/hyung/noona/sunbae* have no clean equivalents. Policy: **preserve in subtitles** (fandom already knows them and expects them); **naturalize in dubs** (a dub cannot carry a glossary).

---

## 4. Subtitles: the systematically underfunded asset

Subtitles are 3–4% of localization spend and drive a disproportionate share of first-episode abandonment. Three upgrades, all cheap:

1. **Kill the English pivot.** Translating Korean → English → Spanish/Arabic/Thai compounds error and strips register. Direct Korean-source translation costs ~20–30% more and is the highest-ROI quality spend available.
2. **Two subtitle registers per language where volume justifies it.** "Standard" (naturalized, tight reading speed) and **"Fan-grade"** (honorifics preserved, Korean terms retained, optional cultural notes). Fan-grade is what fansub groups actually produce and what the core audience prefers. Offering it officially is the cheapest possible anti-piracy measure — you are competing with free by matching its *quality attribute*, not just its price.
3. **A subtitle feedback loop.** In-player "report a translation" tied to timecode, routed to the language lead, with a 14-day patch cycle. Fandoms will QC your catalog for free if you give them a channel; if you don't, they'll do it on X with screenshots.

---

## 5. Cultural sensitivity: one gate, three permitted interventions

The pressure to edit comes from three directions — regulatory (Indonesia, Gulf states, Vietnam, India), advertiser, and reflexive corporate caution. Policy:

**Permitted interventions, in order of preference:**

| # | Intervention | When | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Context, not cuts** — enhanced ratings descriptors, pre-roll historical context card, in-app companion notes, glossary | Default response to *all* sensitivity concerns | Low |
| 2 | **Placement & scheduling** — parental controls tiering, non-promotion in specific markets, Ramadan/holiday calendar shifts, avoiding a title's placement adjacent to a sensitive news cycle | When a title is legal but frictional | Near-zero |
| 3 | **Compliance version** — a distinct, labeled, legally-required cut for a named regulator | Only when the alternative is non-availability of the title, and only with rights-holder consent | High |

**Never permitted:** silent edits, unlabeled versions, pre-emptive self-censorship absent a regulatory requirement, or altering historical depiction to please a third-country audience.

**The specific Korean sensitivity map** — these need a standing advisory function, not case-by-case panic:

- **Japanese colonial period, comfort women, Dokdo:** high salience in Japan and among Korean-diaspora audiences; sub/dub translation choices here are politically read. Translate literally; do not soften.
- **North Korea, defection, DMZ narratives:** sensitive in China-adjacent distribution, and emotionally live for Korean audiences. No editorializing in metadata/synopses.
- **Vietnam War-era content:** significant sensitivity in Vietnam.
- **Alcohol, gambling, shamanism, LGBTQ storylines, physical intimacy:** the primary friction set for Gulf states, Indonesia, Malaysia, and parts of MENA. This is where intervention #3 is most often demanded — resist to #1/#2 first.
- **Religion:** Korean content depicts Christianity, Buddhism, and folk shamanism with a casualness that reads differently in majority-Muslim markets. Ratings descriptors, not cuts.
- **Historical dramas (사극):** the largest comprehension gap globally. Dynasty, rank, and title systems need a glossary or the audience bounces in ten minutes. Sageuk is where the context layer pays for itself.

**Advisory structure:** a small central cultural-standards team + paid regional advisory panels (MENA, SEA, LatAm, Europe) + Korean-side liaison who represents the creator's intent. The Korean production community talks to each other; a reputation for mangling or censoring content raises your acquisition costs on the next slate. **Localization quality is a supply-side competitive weapon**, not just a demand-side one.

---

## 6. Regional playbooks

| Region | Dub posture | Subtitle posture | Cultural gate | Marketing archetype | Fandom shape |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Brazil** | T1/T2 pt-BR, near-mandatory; respect the dubbing industry's stature — cast recognized voices | Fan-grade available | Low | **Star + emotion.** Actor-led, telenovela-adjacent positioning, TikTok edits | Huge, warm, meme-native, very high clip-sharing |
| **Spanish LatAm** | T2 neutral-LatAm dub as base; Mexican-inflected for comedy | Fan-grade | Low | Star + genre hybrid | Twitter/X-organized, strong fan-translation culture |
| **MENA** | Dialect decision is strategic: **MSA for prestige/sageuk, Egyptian or Khaleeji for contemporary rom-com** — test per genre | Arabic subs critical; RTL typography QC often neglected | **Highest.** Compliance versions likely for a minority of titles; Ramadan scheduling is a major opportunity | Family co-viewing + values-adjacent themes (family duty, filial piety travel extremely well) | Fast-growing, female-skewed, Instagram/X, high tolerance for subs |
| **SEA – Thailand, Philippines, Indonesia, Vietnam** | Highest dub demand density outside LatAm; Thai and Tagalog dubs are conversion machines | Essential; Bahasa and Vietnamese quality currently weakest in industry | Moderate (Indonesia regulatory; Vietnam historical) | **Star + fan-event.** Talent visits, meet-and-greets, mall activations still outperform digital | The most intense fandoms globally; K-pop crossover; organized, transnational, will mobilize |
| **Europe – FIGS + Türkiye + Poland** | Germany/Italy/Spain/France: T2 dub for hits only. Türkiye: strong dub demand.
